# Towards self-driving codebases

![](/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Favatars%2Fwilson-lin.jpeg&w=48&q=70)

Wilson Lin · 19 min read

![Towards self-driving codebases](/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fog%2Fblog-self-driving-codebases-og-r2.png&w=1920&q=70)

### Table of Contents

↑

-   [Background](#background)
-   [From single to multi-agent](#from-single-to-multi-agent)
-   [Self-coordination](#self-coordination)
-   [Adding structure and roles](#adding-structure-and-roles)
-   [Observing and hill-climbing](#observing-and-hill-climbing)
-   [Continuous executor](#continuous-executor)
-   [Ensuring freshness](#ensuring-freshness)
-   [Pathological behaviors](#pathological-behaviors)
-   [The final system design](#the-final-system-design)

-   [Removing the integrator](#removing-the-integrator)
-   [Throughput and tradeoffs](#throughput-and-tradeoffs)
-   [Commit correctness](#commit-correctness)
-   [Synchronization overhead](#synchronization-overhead)
-   [Infrastructure learnings](#infrastructure-learnings)
-   [Specifying intent to agents](#specifying-intent-to-agents)
-   [Optimizing prompts](#optimizing-prompts)
-   [System design learnings](#system-design-learnings)
-   [Conclusion](#conclusion)

We're excited by the reaction to our research on scaling [long-running autonomous coding](/blog/scaling-agents).

This work started as internal research to push the limits of the current models. As part of the research, we created a new agent harness to orchestrate many thousands of agents and observe their behavior. By last month, our system was stable enough to run continuously for one week, making the vast majority of the commits to our research project (a web browser). This browser was not intended to be used externally and we expected the code to have imperfections.

However, even with quirks, the fact that thousands of agents could work together to produce work that was almost entirely runnable without human intervention felt like a milestone worth sharing. Since then, we've continued our research, and we wanted to go more in-depth on how the harness was built.

We're also making part of this research available to try for some users.

## [#](#background)Background

Our research project started as a personal side project of mine.

A browser felt like an interesting benchmark. It was complex enough to reveal limitations with frontier models, and there are many different subsystems that needed to work together.

My initial plan was to support rendering web pages without JavaScript support. I started by prompting Opus 4.5, asking it to write a detailed plan for building a browser engine. I would repeatedly nudge it to "keep going" to see how far it would go on the plan.

This failed quickly. The model lost track of what it was doing, frequently stopped to proclaim success despite being far from it, and got stuck on complex implementation details. But it showed signs of deep knowledge and intelligence. It could write good code in small pieces.

The core issue was that the browser was too overwhelming of a task and needed to be broken down into subtasks. Next, I had the agent plan out a dependency graph of major work that agents could take up in parallel. Agents were manually spawned for tasks and nudged when they stopped. This increased the throughput, but the results weren't much better. Agents couldn't communicate with each other or provide feedback on the project as a whole. The system needed to be more dynamic.

Meanwhile, GPT-5.1 (and later GPT-5.2) began showing better results for their ability to follow instructions precisely. This seemed like a good fit for long-running agents, so we updated our harness to use OpenAI models based on these experiments.

At this point, the harness could build a simple version of the web browser without JavaScript, but building a complete browser engine with one agent would be prohibitively slow.

This started our next round of research. Could we spend 10x more on compute to get 10x more meaningful throughput?

## [#](#from-single-to-multi-agent)From single to multi-agent

We started a new repository with a simple Rust-based harness.

Rather than dealing with the complexity of distributed systems, we instead ran the harness on a single large Linux VM (Virtual Machine) with lots of resources. To control the harness, we would SSH into the VM and use a simple terminal interface.

We spent more time up front on proper observability into the system. We logged all agent messages, system actions, and command outputs, with timestamps so we could analyze and replay sessions. This was not only helpful for us to manually review, but also for piping back into Cursor to sift through large amounts of data and quickly find patterns.

### [#](#self-coordination)Self-coordination

Our first multi-agent idea was the most simple: have agents with equal roles use a shared state file to see what others are working on, decide what to work on, and update the file.

![Self-coordination diagram showing agents connecting to a shared coordination file](/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fautonomy-diagram-1-3.png&w=1920&q=70)![Self-coordination diagram showing agents connecting to a shared coordination file](/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fautonomy-diagram-1-3-dark.png&w=1920&q=70)

We would be the least prescriptive about what to do and instead let the agents figure out how to self-coordinate. This failed quickly.

The coordination file quickly created more problems. Agents held locks for too long, forgot to release them, tried to lock or unlock when it was illegal to, and in general didn't understand the significance of holding a lock on the coordination file. Locking is easy to get wrong and narrowly correct, and more prompting didn't help.

Locking also caused too much contention. 20 agents would slow to the throughput of 1-3 with most time spent waiting on locks. We tried giving agents a tool to explicitly wait on another agent's work, but they rarely used it. We also tried a lockless optimistic concurrency control approach, which reduced overhead but didn't eliminate confusion.

The lack of structure between agents meant no single agent took on big, complex tasks. They avoided contention and conflict, opting for smaller and safer changes versus taking responsibility for the project as a whole.

## [#](#adding-structure-and-roles)Adding structure and roles

Next, we separated roles to gives the agents ownership and accountability:

![Structured roles diagram showing Planner, Executor, Workers, and Judge in a pipeline](/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fautonomy-diagram-2-3.png&w=1920&q=70)![Structured roles diagram showing Planner, Executor, Workers, and Judge in a pipeline](/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fautonomy-diagram-2-3-dark.png&w=1920&q=70)

A planner would first lay out the exact approach and deliverables to make progress toward the user's instructions. This would be handed to an executor, who became the sole lead agent responsible for ensuring the plan was achieved completely. The executor could spawn tasks for workers, which provided linear scaling and throughput.

For continued movement and accountability, an independent judge ran after the executor finished to determine whether it completed and whether another iteration should run. This resolved many coordination issues. Having a single role dedicated to owning and overseeing execution allowed workers to focus narrowly on their task while the overall system still delivered.

### [#](#observing-and-hill-climbing)Observing and hill-climbing

Landing on this design required close observation of the system.

If there was a major problem, it would tend to occur repeatedly and across many agents and tool calls. For example, we noticed there was too much contention because many agents were running `git restore` at once. We used Cursor to analyze logs and compare them against our prompts to understand why behavior didn't match expectations.

Ultimately, we found this system to be bottlenecked by the slowest worker. It was too rigid.

Doing all planning upfront also made it hard for the system to dynamically readjust as new issues were discovered. Some agents would end up going in counterproductive directions, unable to self-correct until the next iteration of the loop.

## [#](#continuous-executor)Continuous executor

The next version removed the independent planner.

The executor could now also plan how to deliver the goal in addition to spawning tasks. Since it was the sole agent, it didn't need to write a plan anywhere, stick to one static unchanging plan, or rigidly wait for all workers.

### [#](#ensuring-freshness)Ensuring freshness

To ensure agents across all roles wouldn't drift over long periods of time, we introduced freshness mechanisms:

1.  A `scratchpad.md` should be frequently rewritten versus being appended to.
2.  Individual agents should automatically summarize when reaching context limits.
3.  We added self-reflection and alignment reminders to the system prompts.
4.  Agents were encouraged to pivot and challenge assumptions at any time.

The system was now highly dynamic and flexible: it could proactively explore code, reconsider decisions, manage workers, interleave tasks, and continuously reflect the latest information. We found agents were reasonably good at following instructions to completion, so the judge was removed to keep the system simple.

![Continuous executor diagram showing an infinite executor loop with workers](/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fautonomy-diagram-3-3.png&w=1920&q=70)![Continuous executor diagram showing an infinite executor loop with workers](/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fautonomy-diagram-3-3-dark.png&w=1920&q=70)

### [#](#pathological-behaviors)Pathological behaviors

Despite these improvements, the continuous executor started exhibiting pathological behaviors. It would sleep randomly, stop running agents, do work itself, refuse to plan and spawn more than a few narrowly focused tasks, not properly merge worker changes, and claim premature completion.

We found it was being given too many roles and objectives simultaneously, including: plan, explore, research, spawn tasks, check on workers, review code, perform edits, merge outputs, and judge if the loop is done. In retrospect, it makes sense it was overwhelmed.

## [#](#the-final-system-design)The final system design

The final design incorporates all of our learnings:

1.  A root planner owns the entire scope of the user's instructions. It's responsible for understanding the current state and delivering specific, targeted tasks that would progress toward the goal. It does no coding itself. It's not aware of whether its tasks are being picked up or by whom.
2.  When a planner feels its scope can be subdivided, it spawns subplanners that fully own the delegated narrow slice, taking full ownership in a similar way but only for that slice. This is recursive.
3.  Workers pick up tasks and are solely responsible for driving them to completion. They're unaware of the larger system. They don't communicate with any other planners or workers. They work on their own copy of the repo, and when done, they write up a single handoff that the system submits to the planner that requested the task.

Interestingly, this does represent how some software teams operate today.

![Final system design showing recursive planners, sub-planners, workers, and git](/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fautonomy-diagram-4-3.png&w=1920&q=70)![Final system design showing recursive planners, sub-planners, workers, and git](/marketing-static/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fptht05hbb1ssoooe.public.blob.vercel-storage.com%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fautonomy-diagram-4-3-dark.png&w=1920&q=70)

Subplanners increase throughput by rapidly fanning out workers while ensuring the whole system remains fully owned and responsible by an agent. This also helped with large projects and tasks where a single planner would otherwise get overwhelmed and develop tunnel vision.

The handoff contains not just what was done, but important notes, concerns, deviations, findings, thoughts, and feedback. The planner receives this as a follow-up message. This keeps the system in continuous motion: even if a planner is "done," it continues to receive updates, pulls in the latest repo, and can continue to plan and make subsequent decisions.

All agents have this mechanism, which allows the system to remain incredibly dynamic and self-converging, propagating information up the chain to owners with increasingly global views, without the overhead of global synchronization or cross-talk.

### [#](#removing-the-integrator)Removing the integrator

We originally added an integrator for central globally-aware quality control and to remove contention from too many workers trying to push, rebase, resolve conflicts, and merge simultaneously.

It quickly became an obvious bottleneck. There were hundreds of workers and one gate (i.e. "red tape") that all work must pass through. We tried prompt changes, but ultimately decided it was unnecessarily and could be removed to simplify the system.

## [#](#throughput-and-tradeoffs)Throughput and tradeoffs

The system peaked at ~1,000 commits per hour across 10M tool calls over a period of one week. Once the system started, it didn't require any intervention from us.

There were intentional tradeoffs to achieve this throughput.

### [#](#commit-correctness)Commit correctness

When we required 100% correctness before every single commit, it caused major serialization and slowdowns of effective throughput. Even a single small error, like an API change or typo, would cause the whole system to grind to a halt. Workers would go outside their scope and start fixing irrelevant things. Many agents would pile on and trample each other trying to fix the same issue.

This behavior wasn't helpful or necessary. Allowing some slack means agents can trust that other issues will get fixed by fellow agents soon, which is true since the system has effective ownership and delegation over the whole codebase. Errors arise then get fixed quickly. The error rate remains small and constant, perhaps rarely completely clean but steady and manageable, not exploding or deteriorating.

This may indicate that the ideal efficient system accepts some error rate, but a final "green" branch is needed where an agent regularly takes snapshots and does a quick fixup pass before release.

### [#](#synchronization-overhead)Synchronization overhead

Sometimes multiple agents touch the same file or refactor the same code. Instead of trying to stamp these out completely or overengineer a solution, we accept some moments of turbulence and let the system naturally converge and settle over a short period of time.

This spends some extra tokens and creates local contention, but keeps the system overall simpler: easier to align models and not overwhelm them, easier to manage and observe, less friction, and better global productivity. It also avoids overly complex approaches.

## [#](#infrastructure-learnings)Infrastructure learnings

Each multi-agent run ran on its own large machine with ample system resources, to avoid premature complexity around distributed systems. This was a good fit, as most runs would peak at several hundred agents, which typically saturated but did not overprescribe these machines. This architecture made it easier to observe system metrics, and share and copy state where necessary.

After limiting RAM usage of agents, the disk became the hotspot. Especially with a monolith project, hundreds of agents compiling simultaneously would result in many GB/s reads and writes of build artifacts. This had a significant impact on the overall throughput of the harness, which was an interesting lesson: the project structure, architectural decisions, and developer experience can affect token and commit throughput, simply because working with the codebase (e.g. compilation) dominates time, instead of ideally thinking and coding.

There were also constraints and inefficiencies in the general development environment: things that make sense or aren't significant for a single user workspace, can stick out with hundreds of agents doing the same thing on one machine. One trivial way to solve this is to give each agent its own machine. But there are interesting low-hanging opportunities for large efficiency gains just by rethinking and redesigning some of these primitives and tools.

For example, many tools like Git and Cargo use shared locks, largely as a simple concurrency control mechanism. Could bringing well-established mechanisms from concurrent systems like databases make these work just as well in multi-agent systems? All agents have their own copy of the repo, but most files and artifacts are identical; could adding simple copy-on-write and deduplication features, found in more sophisticated production storage systems, bring similar easy wins to a typically "single-user" system without building separate infrastructure?

## [#](#specifying-intent-to-agents)Specifying intent to agents

Instructions given to this multi-agent system were very important.

Initially, we didn't make them our primary goal, but instead aimed for a stable and effective harness. But the significance of instructions became apparent quickly. We were essentially interacting with a typical coding agent, except with orders of magnitude more time and compute. This amplifies everything, including suboptimal and unclear instructions.

Spending more time on the initial instructions makes sense. Ultimately, agents are still agents: trained to follow your instructions strictly, go down those paths, not change or override them, even if they're bad.

We wanted to see success in our research projects, so we altered our initial instructions as the project and harness evolved. We were learning how to build a browser alongside learning how to operate this new multi-agent system, and could see poor or underspecified specifications reflected in the quality of the outputs, which was not due to the harness itself. The harness was merely following our instructions exactly.

Some examples from the browser project:

-   Initially, the instructions focused on implementing specs and squashing bugs. Instructions like "spec implementation" were vague enough that agents would go deep into obscure, rarely used features rather than intelligently prioritizing.
-   We assumed implicitly that there were performance expectations within user-friendly bounds. But it took explicit instructions and enforced timeouts to force agents to balance performance alongside other goals.
-   For complex parts of the system, agents may write code that has memory leaks or causes deadlocks. Humans would notice this, but it wasn't always obvious to agents. Explicit process-based resource management tools were required to allow the system to gracefully recover and be more defensive.

Our first version of the simple browser without JavaScript converged on an architecture that was unfit to evolve into a full browser. This was a failure of the initial specification.

Similarly, while the agents were told the project was a browser from scratch, they still pulled some dependencies they could've implemented themselves, or used as temporary scaffolding while proper implementation was underway. This was oversight in instructions. A later run explicitly laid out the dependency philosophy and which libraries must not be used, which corrected this.

That later run also did a major restructuring into many self-contained crates, moving away from a monolith. The repo was in a heavily broken state, but the multi-agent system converged toward working code in a few days. This showed the system has strong capability to work collaboratively and intelligently, holding across totally broken states instead of degrading further or getting stuck. This run also spent far less time waiting on compilation, running at multiple times more throughput than previously.

Architecture and instructions matter. Agents have immense engineering skill but will follow instructions to the end, good or bad. Finding the balance between overly narrow metrics and unstructured freedom was tricky, as was knowing what was obvious versus what needed explicit mention.

All of this indicates the importance of eliciting, specifying, and understanding intent, which becomes even more significant at this scale. Steerability and observability will be interesting research areas to continue exploring.

## [#](#optimizing-prompts)Optimizing prompts

Prompting was a significant part of the evolution process.

**Most Relevant Evidence**

| Post | Relevant finding |
|---|---|
| [Dynamic context discovery](https://cursor.com/blog/dynamic-context-discovery), Jan 6, 2026 | Large outputs should be externalized losslessly and discovered on demand; compacted chat should remain searchable. |
| [Training Composer for longer horizons](https://cursor.com/blog/self-summarization), Mar 17, 2026 | Compaction works better when the model is trained for self-summarization; current plan/task state must survive compaction. |
| [Improving Cursor’s agent for OpenAI Codex models](https://cursor.com/blog/codex-model-harness), Dec 4, 2025 | Dropping Codex reasoning traces caused a reported 30% CursorBench performance drop. |
| [Continually improving our agent harness](https://cursor.com/blog/continually-improving-agent-harness), Apr 30, 2026 | Static context has mostly been replaced with dynamic retrieval; harnesses and continuation rules need model-specific behavior. |
| [What we’ve learned building cloud agents](https://cursor.com/blog/cloud-agent-lessons), Jun 2, 2026 | Conversation storage should be append-only, durable, and independent of the running agent; retries need logical rewind/supersession. |
| [Towards self-driving codebases](https://cursor.com/blog/self-driving-codebases), Feb 5, 2026 | Current scratch state should be rewritten for freshness, while complete trajectories remain available for replay and analysis. |
| [Fast regex search](https://cursor.com/blog/fast-regex-search), Mar 23, 2026 | Exact search must be fast and fresh; stale search can send agents into expensive recovery loops. |
| [Improving agent with semantic search](https://cursor.com/blog/semsearch), Nov 6, 2025 | Exact and semantic retrieval are complementary, but the published gains concern code search, not transcript search. |
| [How we compare model quality](https://cursor.com/blog/cursorbench), Mar 11, 2026 | Harness changes need realistic long-task evaluation across correctness, efficiency, and interaction behavior. |

## Design Amendments

### 1. Separate three layers of history

Cursor’s append-only system refers to durable storage, not necessarily replaying every stored item to every model.

PRAANA should explicitly separate:

```text
Canonical event history
  Every attempt, tool result, retry, compaction, and supersession

Logical accepted conversation
  Only successful/accepted message and tool protocol units

Model-visible context
  Current handoff + recent real messages + StateGraph + artifact references
```

This means a failed partial model response remains in the audit log but is not shown alongside its successful retry.

### 2. Reasoning continuation becomes a first-class requirement

The reported 30% Codex degradation strongly validates the earlier reasoning-replay discussion.

The planning document should require every provider adapter to declare:

- What reasoning or signature blocks must be replayed
- How tool calls and results must be ordered
- Whether server-side continuation IDs are supported
- Which boundaries are safe for compaction
- Whether continuation survives a model switch
- How retries supersede partial output

Opaque reasoning data belongs in a protected provider-protocol store. It should not be indexed as searchable transcript text.

### 3. Compaction strategy must be model-aware

Cursor’s best self-summarization result used Composer, which was specifically trained with compaction in its reinforcement-learning loop.

Their reported result:

- Approximately 1,000-token self-summaries
- Approximately one-fifth the tokens of their tuned baseline
- A reported 50% reduction in compaction error
- Successful repeated compaction over a 170-turn task
- KV-cache reuse during the summarization request

We cannot assume an arbitrary model will perform the same way.

The selected design is now:

```text
Capability profile:
  Known self-summary model -> active model on the existing cached prefix
  Unknown/weak model       -> configured structured summarizer
```

A more expensive summarizer should not automatically be preferred. Cursor reports one experiment where an expensive summarizer produced negligible quality improvement relative to cost.

### 4. Immutable summaries stay in storage, not all in context

Cursor’s long-running-agent research recommends frequently rewriting current scratch state rather than endlessly appending stale scratchpads.

Our refined design is:

```text
Immutable summary segments
  Durable, provenance-bearing, searchable source-range records

Bounded current handoff
  Model-visible summary of relevant prior segments

StateGraph
  Fresh current tasks, decisions, constraints, errors, and next actions

Recent real messages
  Exact interaction and protocol trail
```

This preserves immutable evidence without filling the prompt with an ever-growing stack of historical summaries.

### 5. Append-only retry semantics need attempt IDs

Cursor’s conversation storage can logically rewind streamed output when a failed step is retried.

PRAANA should append rather than mutate:

```text
assistant_attempt_started
assistant_step
attempt_failed
attempt_superseded
attempt_accepted
turn_committed
```

The logical transcript includes only accepted attempts. This also solves crash recovery and duplicate partial-output problems.

### 6. Artifactization remains correct

Cursor repeatedly confirms the value of writing large outputs somewhere lossless and searchable rather than truncating them.

PRAANA can use the artifact database rather than literal files. The abstraction matters more than the storage mechanism.

Each model-visible artifact preview should include:

```text
artifact ID
tool and command
tool-call ID
content type
token/line count
exit status
bounded preview or tail
content hash
exact retrieval instruction
```

The artifact body must be the post-redaction version and searchable by exact text.

### 7. Start transcript search with exact search and FTS

Cursor’s evidence supports both regex and semantic search for codebases, but it does not establish that semantic transcript search is worth its complexity.

Recommended initial transcript retrieval:

- Exact text and regex
- SQLite FTS/BM25
- Filters by turn, tool, path, event kind, artifact, and summary range
- Stable source event IDs
- Full artifact-body matching

Semantic transcript search remains an experiment, not a Phase 1 requirement.

### 8. StateGraph retention is reinforced

Cursor’s self-summaries explicitly preserve plan state, remaining tasks, and number of previous summaries. Its long-running work also relies on fresh scratch state and structured handoffs.

This supports keeping StateGraph in append mode, with one constraint:

> StateGraph is a reconstructible current-state projection; canonical events remain the source of truth.

Only active StateGraph items should be guaranteed prompt space. Soft/hard entries remain searchable or explicitly retrievable.

### 9. Model switching needs an explicit handoff boundary

Cursor confirms that switching models mid-conversation is difficult because:

- Prompt and tool formats differ
- Previous messages are out of distribution
- Provider caches are lost
- Native reasoning state is not portable
- Summary-based switching can lose details

PRAANA should:

- Prefer one model for a conversation epoch
- Drop incompatible opaque reasoning on switch
- Append a visible model-switch handoff
- Tell the new model which tools are currently available
- Run admission against the new model’s context window
- Keep the full old transcript searchable

Automatic per-turn routing is outside this redesign’s initial scope.

### 10. Tool schemas are another context cost

Dynamic context discovery reports a 46.9% token reduction in MCP-using runs when Cursor replaced always-present tool descriptions with dynamically discoverable definitions.

PRAANA does not need to implement dynamic tool loading in this phase, but the planning document should require:

- Tool-schema tokens included in admission calculations
- Stable tool ordering for caching
- An eventual tool-catalog/loading extension point
- Optional tools not assumed to remain permanently resident

PRAANA’s existing skills pull model already follows this pattern.

## What Does Not Change

The Cursor research does not establish better values than our selected defaults:

```toml
[history]
mode = "append"
compact_at = 0.60
compact_mass_fraction = 0.50
reasoning_replay = "active"
```

However, these should be labeled **initial experimental defaults**, not research-backed constants.

The 50% means eligible historical token mass, excluding:

- System policy
- Tool schemas
- Active StateGraph
- Current user request
- Current incomplete tool cycle
- Required provider continuation state

## Evaluation Amendment

Before declaring append mode superior to engine mode, the planning document should require model-stratified tests.

Measure:

- End-task correctness
- Constraint and open-task recall after compaction
- Unsupported facts introduced by summaries
- Exact-history recovery success
- Duplicate tool calls and file reads
- Lost subgoals
- Invalid provider protocol requests
- Reasoning continuation retained/dropped
- Artifact retrieval rate and usefulness
- Number and cost of compactions
- Input, output, cached, and uncached tokens
- Time to first token and total completion time
- Task performance before and after forced compaction

Run threshold sweeps later:

```text
Trigger: 40%, 50%, 60%, 70%
Compacted eligible mass: 25%, 50%, 75%
```

The selected 60/50 policy remains the starting point.

## Final Architecture

```text
Durable append-only canonical events
        |
        +-> logical accepted conversation
        |
        +-> protected provider reasoning continuation
        |
        +-> lossless searchable artifacts
        |
        +-> immutable summary segments
        |
        +-> fresh StateGraph projection
        |
        +-> bounded model-visible handoff + recent real messages
```

The Cursor review strengthens the direction rather than overturning it. The main correction is that **append-only describes storage**, while the model receives a carefully valid projection of accepted real messages, fresh state, and bounded summaries. We now have enough settled detail to produce the planning document.

Yes, specifically the **StateGraph and checkpoint parts** of engine mode.

A useful mapping is:

| Cursor concept | PRAANA equivalent |
|---|---|
| Full trajectory/log | `events.jsonl` |
| Frequently rewritten scratchpad | StateGraph + session checkpoint |
| Older summaries | Summary segments |
| Search old details | `search_session_log` / artifacts |
| Recent conversation | Real appended messages |

The scratchpad contains only the **current truth**:

```text
Current goal
Current plan
Open tasks
Active constraints
Latest decisions
Unresolved errors
Next steps
```

When something changes, Cursor rewrites that state rather than appending:

```text
Old: Implement SQLite storage
New: SQLite approach failed; use filesystem storage
```

This avoids showing both statements as if they were still valid.

- StateGraph tasks, decisions, constraints, and notes
- Active/soft/hard tiers
- Turn digests
- Checkpoint reconciliation
- Current errors and plans

- Scores historical context
- Runs BM25 and semantic ranking
- Allocates token bands
- Selects artifacts every turn
- Applies density weighting
- Recompiles a different context every turn

Cursor’s scratchpad idea does **not** imply all that machinery. It is simply a small mutable current-state document alongside durable history.

So our proposed append mode is effectively:

> Keep the strongest part of engine mode, the fresh structured state, but remove automatic per-turn historical curation.

The final design becomes:

```text
events.jsonl                = complete immutable history
summary segments            = compressed historical evidence
StateGraph/current handoff  = frequently refreshed scratchpad
recent real messages        = exact conversation trail
artifact/search tools       = recover details on demand
```

This is why retaining StateGraph in both modes is valuable. It protects active goals and constraints from compaction without requiring the full scoring engine. The StateGraph/current handoff should be placed near the end of the model-visible context so updates do not invalidate the stable prompt prefix more than necessary.

I’m thinking about whether SQLite is truly necessary. Technically, there might not be a hard need to keep it, but I recommend maintaining it because the system relies on it heavily. Short answer:

- **Embedding model:** no longer required for the default history mode.
- **SQLite:** still useful and should remain.

## Embedding Model

Today embeddings serve two purposes:

1. Engine-mode semantic scoring for deciding what context to inject.
2. Cognitive Memory semantic recall across sessions.

The new append design removes the first requirement entirely. Transcript and artifact search can initially use:

- Exact text/regex
- SQLite FTS
- BM25
- Tool/path/turn filters

Therefore, history mode can work without downloading an embedding model.

Embeddings become optional:

```toml
[history]
mode = "append"

[memory]
embedder = "none" # keyword/FTS recall

# Optional:
# embedder = "auto" # semantic Cognitive Memory recall
```

Engine mode can enable embeddings when available, while still falling back to BM25 if unavailable.

This removes the ONNX model download and native embedding runtime from the default path. The tradeoff is weaker paraphrase-based cross-session recall. We should benchmark keyword-only Cognitive Memory before deciding whether embeddings should be disabled by default.

## SQLite

SQLite remains valuable for:

- Full artifact storage
- Exact/FTS search over artifact contents
- Artifact metadata and hashes
- Summary-segment metadata
- Search indexes
- Scorecard and evaluation data
- Cross-session Cognitive Memory
- Atomic compaction/index transactions

The cleaner architecture would be:

```text
~/.praana/sessions/<id>/
  events.jsonl       Canonical ordered event history
  history.db         Session artifacts, FTS index, summaries, projections
  meta.json          Session metadata

~/.praana/
  memory.db          Cross-session Cognitive Memory only
```

A per-session `history.db` is better than the current shared context-engine database because:

- Artifact ownership is naturally session-scoped.
- Deleting a session deletes its artifacts.
- No cross-session TTL mistakes.
- Search remains local and fast.
- Resume does not depend on a global shared database.
- Engine and append modes can share the same history store.

`events.jsonl` remains the canonical protocol/audit history. SQLite is the searchable materialized index plus the canonical store for large artifact bodies.

## Recommended Decision

```text
Embedding model:
  Optional capability, not required by history mode

SQLite:
  Keep, but simplify into per-session history.db + global memory.db

Default history search:
  Exact + regex + FTS/BM25

Optional later:
  Semantic transcript search and semantic Cognitive Memory
```

So the new design removes the **need for embeddings**, but not the need for structured local storage. Removing SQLite would mostly replace a reliable built-in database with more complicated file indexing, locking, deduplication, and transaction code.

77: /**

79:  * TODO(scorecard): placeholder — replace with real telemetry signal (tests passed,

83: export function isSessionGood(
84:   reason: string,
85:   events: Array<{ type: string; result?: unknown }> | undefined,
86: ): boolean {
87:   if (reason !== "normal") return false;
88:   if (!events || events.length === 0) return true; // no events → assume good
89:   // NOTE: sessions with only user/agent messages (no tool calls) return false here,
90:   // meaning used entries get neutral rather than boosted usefulness. This is intentional
91:   // for the placeholder — a tool-free session gives no signal about memory utility.
92:   // TODO(scorecard): replace with real telemetry once ADR-005 C1 / #99 delivers a
93:   // reliable success signal that covers conversational sessions too.
94:   return events.some((e) => {
95:     if (e.type !== "tool_result") return false;
96:     if (e.result && typeof e.result === "object" && "ok" in e.result) {
97:       return (e.result as { ok: boolean }).ok === true;
98:     }
99:     return false;
100:   });

141: function lexicalMatchScore(
142:   entry: MemoryEntry,
143:   terms: string[],
144:   rankScore: number,
145: ): number {
146:   if (terms.length === 0) return 0;
147: 
148:   const content = entry.content.toLowerCase();
149:   const matched = terms.filter((term) => content.includes(term)).length;
150:   if (matched === 0) return 0;
151: 
152:   const coverage = matched / terms.length;
153:   return 0.6 + coverage * 0.3 + rankScore * 0.1;
154: }

156: export class MemoryStore {
157:   private db: Database;
158:   readonly embedder: Embedder | null;
159:   private summarizer: SummarizerLLM | null;

161:   private sessionId: string = "";

163:    *  the session-start prune handles that case, so the throttle is best-effort. */
164:   private lastGrowthPruneCount = 0;

166:   private reembedding = false;
167:   private reembedPromise: Promise<void> | null = null;
168:   private readonly logger: PraanaLogger;
169: 
170:   constructor(opts: {
171:     dbPath: string;
172:     embedder: Embedder | null;
173:     summarizer?: SummarizerLLM | null;
174:     logger?: PraanaLogger;
175:     needsReembed?: boolean;
176:     embeddingBackend?: string;
177:   }) {

179:       opts.dbPath,
180:       opts.embedder?.dim ?? EMBEDDING_DIM,
181:       opts.embeddingBackend,

184:     this.embedder = opts.embedder;
185:     this.summarizer = opts.summarizer ?? null;

188:       this.reembedPromise = this.reembedAllEntries();
189:     }
190:   }
191:

193:     this.db.close();
194:   }
195: 
196:   /** Get the summarizer LLM (may be null if summarizer is disabled). */
197:   getSummarizer(): SummarizerLLM | null {
198:     return this.summarizer;
199:   }
200:

202:     const row = this.db.prepare("SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM entries").get() as { c: number } | undefined;
203:     return row?.c ?? 0;
204:   }
205:

207:   countPendingReinforcementsUsed(): number {
208:     if (!this.sessionId) return 0;
209:     return countPendingReinforcementsUsed(this.db, this.sessionId);
210:   }
211: 
212:   // ---- Session lifecycle ----
213: 
214:   async sessionStart(ctx: SessionContext): Promise<Digest> {
215:     await this.waitForReembed();
216: 
217:     this.sessionId = ulid();
218:     this.defaultScopes = this.buildDefaultScopes(ctx);
219: 
220:     const reconciled = await this.reconcileDuplicatesIfNeeded();
221:     if (reconciled.entriesRemoved > 0) {
222:       this.logger.child("memory").info(
223:         `Reconciled ${reconciled.clustersMerged} duplicate ${reconciled.clustersMerged === 1 ? "cluster" : "clusters"} (${reconciled.entriesRemoved} ${reconciled.entriesRemoved === 1 ? "entry" : "entries"} removed)`,
224:       );
225:     }
226: 
227:     const pruned = await this.prune();
228:     if (pruned > 0) {
229:       this.logger.child("memory").info(`Pruned ${pruned} stale Layer 1 ${pruned === 1 ? "entry" : "entries"}`);
230:     }
231: 
232:     startSessionRow(this.db, {
233:       id: this.sessionId,
234:       agent: ctx.agent,
235:       user_id: ctx.user_id,
236:       context_id: ctx.context_id,
237:       started_at: ctx.time,
238:     });
239: 
240:     // Stamp the digest's entries as surfaced for THIS session. The digest is
241:     // the primary surfacing path (injected into the system prompt), so its
242:     // entries must count toward the M2 utility loop and the M4 distinct-session
243:     // confirmation gate — not just entries the agent re-queries via recall().
244:     return this.buildDigest(ctx, ctx.recall_min_score, { stampSurfaced: true });
245:   }
246: 
247:   async sessionEnd(
248:     reason: string,
249:     events?: SessionEvent[],
250:     agentsContext?: string,
251:   ): Promise<{ learningsStored: number }> {
252:     const now = Date.now();
253: 
254:     // Determine session-success bit for utility updates.
255:     // TODO(scorecard): placeholder — replace with real scorecard signal (ADR-005 C1 / #99).
256:     const sessionGood = isSessionGood(reason, events);
257: 
258:     // Fetch surfaced entries with content in one JOIN — no N+1 getEntryById calls.
259:     const surfacedWithContent = getSurfacedEntriesWithContent(this.db, this.sessionId);
260: 
261:     // Track whether learnings were already stored by the combined call below,
262:     // so we don't make a redundant second LLM call at session end.
263:     let learningsExtracted = false;
264:     let learningsStored = 0;
265: 
266:     if (surfacedWithContent.length > 0) {
267:       let usedIds: Set<string>;
268: 
269:       if (this.summarizer && events && events.length > 0) {
270:         try {
271:           // Single combined LLM call: returns both usedIds and learnings.
272:           // Storing learnings here avoids a second extractLearnings call below.
273:           const result = await extractLearnings(this.summarizer, events, surfacedWithContent, {
274:             projectContext: agentsContext,
275:           });
276:           usedIds = result.usedIds;
277:           for (const l of result.learnings) {
278:             await this.storeLearning(l);
279:           }
280:           learningsStored = result.learnings.length;
281:           learningsExtracted = true;
282:         } catch {
283:           // Summarizer failed — fall back to co-occurrence for usedIds;
284:           // learningsExtracted stays false so the fallback call below runs.
285:           usedIds = usedIdsByCooccurrence(events, surfacedWithContent);
286:         }
287:       } else {
288:         usedIds = usedIdsByCooccurrence(events ?? [], surfacedWithContent);
289:       }
290: 
291:       // Mark used in pending_reinforcements before flush
292:       for (const { id } of surfacedWithContent) {
293:         markReinforcementUsed(
294:           this.db,
295:           id,
296:           this.sessionId,
297:           usedIds.has(id),
298:         );
299:       }
300: 
301:       // Stamp the session-good flag on all pending rows for this session
302:       if (sessionGood) {
303:         this.db
304:           .prepare(
305:             "UPDATE pending_reinforcements SET good = 1 WHERE session_id = ?",
306:           )
307:           .run(this.sessionId);
308:       }
309:     }
310: 
311:     // M4: Record each surfaced entry as confirmed-in-this-session for the
312:     // distinct-session promotion gate. Done BEFORE flushReinforcements because
313:     // that call deletes pending_reinforcements; the confirmation history is
314:     // what feeds the deterministic gate. Pending rows are still the per-session
315:     // bookkeeping; confirmations is the Cognitive Memory history.
316:     if (surfacedWithContent.length > 0) {
317:       for (const { id } of surfacedWithContent) {
318:         recordConfirmation(this.db, id, this.sessionId, now);
319:       }
320:     }
321: 
322:     // Flush: validity reinforcement + utility updates (two passes)
323:     flushReinforcements(this.db, this.sessionId);
324: 
325:     // M4: Apply the deterministic Layer 1 → Layer 2 promotion gate.
326:     // Runs after flush so validity reinforcement has already landed, but
327:     // promotion is purely a separate concern (distinct-session count + validity).
328:     this.applyPromotionGate(now);
329: 
330:     endSessionRow(this.db, this.sessionId, now, reason);
331: 
332:     // Extract learnings if not already stored by the combined call above.
333:     // Runs when: (a) no entries were surfaced, or (b) the combined call errored.
334:     if (!learningsExtracted && events && events.length > 0 && this.summarizer) {
335:       try {
336:         const result = await extractLearnings(this.summarizer, events, undefined, {
337:           projectContext: agentsContext,
338:         });
339:         for (const l of result.learnings) {
340:           await this.storeLearning(l);
341:         }
342:         learningsStored = result.learnings.length;
343:       } catch (err) {
344:         if (isAbortLikeError(err)) {
345:           this.logger.child("memory").warn("Session-end summarizer aborted; skipping learnings for this session");
346:           return { learningsStored: 0 };
347:         }
348:         throw err;
349:       }
350:     }
351: 
352:     return { learningsStored };
353:   }

355:   /**
356:    * Compress a batch of old turns into episodic facts.
357:    * Returns the number of facts stored.
358:    */
359:   async compressTurns(events: SessionEvent[]): Promise<number> {

The current `memory/summarizer.ts` should be divided: the history compaction summarizer will move to the core `history/compactor`, while memory learning extraction will stay as a plugin. It’s fine for the plugin’s full lifecycle to utilize the host LLM. Plus, the engine's deterministic turn digest will remain separate, which is a good thing!

This creates a cleaner architecture and removes Cognitive Memory’s dependencies from PRAANA’s default path.

## Final Boundary

### Core PRAANA

Core owns everything required for a session to function:

- Canonical append-only transcript
- Logical accepted conversation projection
- Real provider messages
- Provider reasoning continuation
- Current-session resume
- History compaction
- StateGraph
- Artifact storage and retrieval
- Current-session history search
- Tool execution
- Scorecard and telemetry

### Memory Plugin

A memory plugin owns everything cross-session:

- Learning extraction
- Storage backend
- Recall and ranking
- Startup digest
- Project/global scopes
- Deduplication
- Confidence and usefulness
- Reinforcement
- Consolidation and decay
- Optional embeddings
- Session-end learning
- Pinning and retraction

The core should know nothing about SQLite rows, vector dimensions, embedding migrations, or memory confidence formulas.

## Default Behavior

```toml
[memory]
plugin = "none"
```

With no plugin:

- No global `memory.db`
- No embedding model
- No model-weight download
- No session-end memory summarization
- No injected cross-session digest
- No `recall`/`remember` tools
- History compaction still works
- Resume and session-history search still work
- StateGraph still works

Users can later opt into the first-party implementation:

```toml
[memory]
plugin = "builtin:sqlite"

[memory.options]
embedder = "none" # FTS/BM25 only

# Optional semantic recall:
# embedder = "auto"
```

## Plugin Contract

A narrow contract would look approximately like:

```ts
export interface MemoryPlugin {
  id: string;
  apiVersion: 1;

  open(host: MemoryPluginHost, options: unknown): Promise<MemorySession>;
}

export interface MemorySession {
  capabilities: MemoryCapabilities;

  start(context: MemorySessionContext): Promise<MemoryBootstrap>;
  recall(query: string, options?: RecallOptions): Promise<RecallResult>;
  remember(input: RememberInput): Promise<RememberResult>;
  retract?(id: string): Promise<void>;
  end(input: MemorySessionEndInput): Promise<MemorySessionEndResult>;
  stats?(): Promise<MemoryStats>;
  close(): Promise<void>;
}
```

The host exposes only narrow infrastructure:

```ts
export interface MemoryPluginHost {
  complete(request: MemoryLlmRequest): Promise<string>;
  log(level: LogLevel, message: string): void;
  now(): number;
}
```

This lets the plugin own its extraction prompts and logic while PRAANA retains provider credentials and LLM transport.

## Data Exposed To Plugins

A memory plugin may receive:

- Accepted visible transcript
- Current StateGraph snapshot
- Project/user/agent scope identifiers
- Redacted artifact summaries and references
- Session outcome signals
- Explicit memories submitted through `remember`

It should not receive:

- Superseded model attempts
- Opaque reasoning signatures
- Encrypted reasoning items
- Provider credentials
- Full internal `Session`
- Raw unredacted artifacts
- Tool execution handles

This keeps provider continuation and sensitive infrastructure outside the plugin boundary.

## Core Tool Ownership

The plugin should not register arbitrary tool schemas initially. Core defines stable `recall`, `remember`, and `retract_memory` tools and delegates them to the configured plugin when supported.

Benefits:

- Stable prompt/tool schemas
- Consistent UX between plugins
- Capability-based registration
- Easier validation and security
- Plugins cannot silently add dangerous tools

When no plugin exists, those tools are simply absent.

## Important Decoupling Work

Several current dependencies must move:

- `Session.memoryStore: MemoryStore` becomes `MemorySession | null`.
- `turn.ts` must stop reading `session.memoryStore?.embedder`.
- Engine semantic scoring gets its own optional embedding capability or uses BM25.
- Skill usefulness moves out of `memory.db` into the session/telemetry database.
- Scorecard stops opening the concrete memory SQLite database directly.
- Artifact promotion becomes a plugin concern handled during `MemorySession.end()`.
- History compaction moves out of `src/memory/summarizer.ts` into a core history compactor.
- Cross-session learning extraction remains in the SQLite memory plugin.

This is necessary because current code directly couples memory into `src/session.ts:1584-1606`, `src/turn.ts:507-508,641`, and skill ranking at `src/session.ts:1816-1828`.

## Failure Behavior

Memory must always fail soft:

```text
Plugin missing         -> start without memory
Plugin initialization  -> log warning, disable for session
Recall timeout         -> return unavailable, continue
Session-end failure    -> preserve session, skip learning
Plugin crash           -> never affect transcript/resume
```

Core history compaction must never depend on memory-plugin availability.

## First Implementation

The chosen approach is:

1. Define the plugin API and contract tests.
2. Convert the existing MemoryStore implementation into `builtin:sqlite`.
3. Keep it compiled into PRAANA initially.
4. Default configuration remains `plugin = "none"`.
5. Stabilize the contract through internal use.
6. Add external package/path loading later.

This avoids prematurely solving package installation, arbitrary-code security, standalone-binary loading, plugin version resolution, and dependency isolation.

## Resulting Storage

```text
~/.praana/sessions/<id>/
  events.jsonl        Core canonical transcript
  history.db          Core artifacts, FTS, summaries, projections
  meta.json           Core session metadata

Optional memory plugin:
  ~/.praana/memory.db Plugin-owned cross-session data
```

A different future plugin could use Markdown files, Postgres, a remote service, an MCP server, or no embeddings at all. Core PRAANA would not change.

This should be incorporated into the planning document as a separate **Pluggable Cognitive Memory** section. It cleanly removes global memory and embedding requirements from the default installation while preserving robust current-session context management.

# Assessment

## Recommendation

Do **not** begin with a full Rust rewrite while simultaneously redesigning conversation history and cross-session memory.

The best path is:

1. **Stabilize the new message/history and memory-plugin contracts in TypeScript first**, but make those contracts language-neutral.
2. **Split host-owned session/context persistence from plugin-owned memory persistence.**
3. Build a **Rust headless core in parallel**, using the existing TypeScript implementation as a differential oracle.
4. Keep the OpenTUI/Solid UI during core migration.
5. Reassess a Ratatui rewrite only after the Rust core has parity.

A full-Rust end state is defensible because PRAANA has no users, no external compatibility burden, and already contains reusable Rust. But a big-bang rewrite now would conflate three independent changes:

- language/runtime,
- conversation semantics,
- memory architecture.

That would make regressions difficult to attribute and invalidate much of PRAANA’s intended engine/classic A/B comparison.

The most important project-specific observation is that PRAANA currently has **four overlapping transcript representations**:

1. Reduced append-only events in `events.jsonl`.
2. Ephemeral provider messages for only the current tool loop.
3. A SQLite turn ledger/checkpoint/digest representation.
4. Separately persisted TUI transcript entries.

The proposed “append-only real messages + compaction + artifacts + reasoning continuation” redesign should unify those before they are reimplemented.

Key references:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/event-log.ts:82`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/turn.ts:121`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/turn.ts:803`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/context-engine/db.ts:58`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/ui/tui/run.tsx:610`

# 2. TypeScript/Bun-specific dependencies and APIs

## Bun coupling is concentrated, but UI and tests are deeply ecosystem-specific

Most runtime code uses Node-compatible APIs and standard Web APIs rather than Bun-specific methods. The migration burden is therefore less about replacing `Bun.*` calls and more about reimplementing TypeScript behavior and its tests.

### OpenTUI, Solid and the JSX transform

The UI is the strongest TypeScript/Bun lock-in:

- `@opentui/core`
- `@opentui/keymap`
- `@opentui/solid`
- `solid-js`
- 47 files under `src/ui/`, including 22 TSX files
- Reactive signals, JSX components, keymap layers, overlays, markdown, textarea and select widgets

References:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/package.json:51`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/ui/tui/run.tsx:80`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/ui/tui/app.tsx:60`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/ui/tui/prompt/index.tsx:65`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/ui/tui/transcript/entries.tsx:106`

The global package needs a custom, package-scoped Bun transform because stock OpenTUI preload skips TSX under `node_modules`:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/bin/praana.js:1`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/bin/opentui-solid-runtime.js:18`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/bunfig.toml:1`

The standalone compiler also depends on `@opentui/solid/bun-plugin` and `Bun.build({ compile: ... })`:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/scripts/compile.ts:190`

A Rust TUI would eliminate this machinery, but it would require recreating:

- auto-growing multiline input,
- paste collapsing,
- path and slash completion,
- keymap focus layers,
- searchable overlays,
- virtual transcript rendering,
- sticky scrolling,
- markdown and syntax highlighting,
- live streamed thinking and assistant blocks,
- setup/login/consent flows,
- debug console behavior.

Ratatui can support all of this, but there is no drop-in translation from Solid/OpenTUI.

### `bun:sqlite`

SQLite is wrapped centrally:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/sqlite.ts:8`

Bun-specific behavior includes:

- `new Database()` for true in-memory databases because `new Database(":memory:")` is explicitly worked around.
- Synchronous `query`, `prepare`, `get`, `all`, `run`, and `exec`.
- Named `$parameter` objects.
- `Buffer`/`Uint8Array` BLOB embeddings.
- `result.changes`.
- WAL, `busy_timeout`, and foreign-key pragmas.

Memory and context-engine database access is extensive:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/memory/db.ts`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/context-engine/db.ts`

The current database uses:

- FTS5 and `bm25(entries_fts)`.
- Float32 embeddings stored as BLOBs.
- Brute-force cosine kNN in TypeScript.
- Additive migrations.
- A fallback table for obsolete `sqlite-vec` installations.

A subtle coupling is that the context-engine DB path is derived from `memory.db`:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/context-engine/index.ts:142`

Therefore artifacts, turn ledgers, scorecards, workflow patterns, skills, and Cognitive Memory currently coexist in or directly depend on the same configured database. That must be separated before memory becomes plugin-owned.

### Other Bun APIs

Production `src/` has little direct Bun usage:

- `Bun.YAML.parse` for `pnpm-workspace.yaml`:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/lsp/workspace-roots.ts:56`
- A `typeof Bun` check when identifying the `bun` executable:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/verify/spawn.ts:15`

Most process execution uses `node:child_process`, not `Bun.spawn`.

Build and packaging scripts use:

- `Bun.build`
- `Bun.spawn`
- `Bun.spawnSync`
- `Bun.file`
- Bun plugin registration

Tests use additional APIs such as `Bun.sleep`, `Bun.which`, and `Bun.spawnSync`.

## Package/global CLI and standalone distribution

Current distribution has two modes:

1. npm/Bun global package:
   - `#!/usr/bin/env bun`
   - imports TypeScript source directly
   - optional `@praana/natives`
2. GitHub standalone release:
   - Bun-compiled executable
   - `praana-natives.node`
   - `praana-natives.json`

References:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/package.json:18`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/bin/praana.js`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/scripts/package-release-binaries.ts:1`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/.github/workflows/release-please.yml:59`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/install.sh:1`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/install.ps1:1`

A full Rust build can reduce this to one executable, assuming the current Rust native capabilities are linked directly. If npm installation is retained, npm would need to become a wrapper/downloader around platform Rust binaries. Given the absence of users, dropping npm as a primary distribution channel would simplify migration.

## LLM drivers and streaming

Despite stale “pi-ai” names and documentation, the current package has **no pi-ai dependency**. PRAANA now has custom, zero-SDK protocol drivers:

- OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions
- OpenAI Responses/Codex
- Anthropic Messages
- Google Gemini/Vertex
- Azure OpenAI
- Bedrock ConverseStream

References:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/index.ts:1`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/drivers/base.ts:10`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/drivers/openai.ts:21`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/drivers/responses.ts:20`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/drivers/anthropic.ts:20`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/drivers/google.ts:19`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/drivers/bedrock.ts:23`

They rely on standard `fetch`, `ReadableStream`, `AbortSignal`, async iterables, a custom SSE parser, custom tool-call accumulation, handcrafted AWS SigV4 and a partial AWS EventStream decoder.

This is favorable for a Rust port because there is no JS provider SDK dependency. It is risky because PRAANA owns all protocol compatibility.

### Reasoning continuation is not currently modeled fully

The canonical message model only has:

- `thinking?: string`
- `thinkingSignature?: string`

Reference:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/types.ts:19`

Persistent `agent_message` events store only text:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/turn.ts:1409`

Prior turns are flattened into the system prompt rather than sent as native provider messages:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/compile-classic.ts:104`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/turn.ts:803`

Provider support is inconsistent:

- Anthropic can re-emit thinking plus signature:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/drivers/anthropic.ts:292`
- OpenAI-compatible history discards thinking:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/drivers/openai.ts:259`
- Responses emits reasoning deltas but its final message does not retain provider reasoning items or continuation identifiers:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/drivers/responses.ts:133`
- Google and Bedrock normalize thinking text but do not retain all provider-native continuation metadata.

The proposed redesign therefore changes the central data model regardless of implementation language.

## OAuth, credentials and config

### Credentials

Credentials are plaintext JSON with atomic writes and Unix `0600` permissions:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/credentials.ts:1`

The store supports static keys and OAuth bundles, with environment fallback. It does not use OS keychains. Windows permissions are best-effort.

### OAuth and cloud credentials

OAuth support is currently mixed:

- GitHub Copilot device flow and token exchange.
- Anthropic and OpenAI Codex “OAuth” are effectively pasted-token adapters.
- Refresh exists as an interface, but most adapters do not refresh.
- AWS support is a hand-implemented partial ambient chain.
- Google ADC supports access tokens or service-account JSON, not the full ADC ecosystem.

References:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/oauth.ts:74`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/oauth.ts:159`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/aws-credentials.ts:13`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/google-adc.ts:8`

### Config

Config loading has important custom semantics:

- Four source layers, global first and local last.
- JSON and TOML.
- Deep recursive object merge.
- Default array replacement.
- Append-and-deduplicate semantics for `shell.allowed_paths` and `risk.allow`.
- Extensive manual validation and warning behavior.
- Environment overrides and path expansion.
- User-defined providers.

Reference:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/config.ts:183`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/config.ts:273`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/config.ts:356`

A generic Rust `config` crate should not be assumed to reproduce these semantics exactly.

## Tests

All TypeScript tests use `bun:test`. The suite makes extensive use of Bun-style mocking:

- roughly 563 `mock(...)` calls,
- 51 `mock.module(...)` calls,
- 27 `spyOn(...)` calls,
- fake fetch responses and streaming `ReadableStream`s,
- temporary SQLite databases and filesystem fixtures.

Examples:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/tests/turn.test.ts`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/tests/tools.test.ts`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/tests/app-controller.test.ts`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/tests/native-llm-wiring.test.ts`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/tests/engine-compiler.test.ts`

The tests are valuable as a behavioral oracle, but they cannot be mechanically translated. Rust will need explicit dependency injection instead of module monkey-patching.

# 3. Existing Rust/native boundary

The existing crate is already the most natural starting point:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/crates/praana-natives/Cargo.toml`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/crates/praana-natives/src/lib.rs`

It implements:

- tree-sitter parsing,
- symbol/import extraction,
- name-based definitions and references,
- gitignore-aware search and file finding,
- tokenization and ONNX embedding via `tract-onnx`.

Dependencies already selected include:

- `tree-sitter` and five grammar crates,
- `ignore`,
- `regex`,
- `globset`,
- `tokenizers`,
- `tract-onnx`,
- `ndarray`.

### Directly reusable code

Approximately **1.7K of the 2.1K Rust lines** are core algorithms that can be absorbed with modest refactoring:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/crates/praana-natives/src/lang.rs`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/crates/praana-natives/src/parse.rs`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/crates/praana-natives/src/symbols.rs`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/crates/praana-natives/src/project.rs`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/crates/praana-natives/src/search.rs`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/crates/praana-natives/src/embed.rs`

The parts to replace are mainly:

- `#[napi]` entry points,
- `#[napi(object)]` DTOs,
- the `.node` loader/version adapter,
- JavaScript-specific error envelopes.

Recommended restructuring:

```text
crates/
  praana-native-core/   # pure Rust algorithms and serde DTOs
  praana-natives-napi/  # temporary N-API wrapper for TypeScript
  praana-core/          # new session/tool/provider core
  praana-cli/           # eventual CLI/TUI
```

This lets TypeScript and Rust use the same search/tree-sitter/embed implementation during migration.

### Immediate benefits of absorption

- Removes N-API serialization and copies, especially `Vec<f64>` embeddings.
- Removes synchronous native calls that currently block Bun’s event loop.
- Allows search/tree-sitter work to run under `spawn_blocking` or dedicated workers.
- Links grammars and ONNX runtime directly into the final executable.
- Eliminates `.node` platform packages and the sidecar manifest in a full-Rust build.

The embedder currently loads the tokenizer and ONNX model on each call:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/crates/praana-natives/src/embed.rs:63`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/crates/praana-natives/src/embed.rs:84`

A Rust core should cache loaded models by model directory.

---

# 4. Rust ecosystem replacements

| Current responsibility | Recommended Rust choices | Project-specific notes |
|---|---|---|
| CLI | `clap` | Reproduce current subcommands, partial session IDs and exit codes with `assert_cmd` tests. |
| TUI | `ratatui` + `crossterm` | Strong ecosystem, but immediate-mode rather than Solid reactive rendering. |
| Textarea/input | `tui-textarea` or a custom editor state | Paste chips, history, autocomplete and focus/keymap behavior will still be custom. |
| Markdown | `pulldown-cmark` plus custom Ratatui spans; optionally `tui-markdown` | Current OpenTUI `<markdown>` handles streaming directly. Verify incremental rendering. |
| Syntax highlighting | `syntect` or tree-sitter highlighting | `syntect` increases binary size and compile time; existing tree-sitter grammars may be reusable. |
| Async runtime | `tokio` | Use structured tasks and `tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken`. |
| HTTP and streaming | `reqwest`, `bytes`, `futures-util` | Keep provider parsers explicit; avoid hiding provider-native reasoning fields. |
| SSE | `eventsource-stream`/`reqwest-eventsource`, or a small owned parser | Given tool-call and reasoning requirements, a well-tested owned parser may be preferable. |
| SQLite | `rusqlite` | Better fit than `sqlx` for the current synchronous, SQLite-specific schema and FTS queries. |
| SQLite distribution | bundled SQLite configured and tested with FTS5 | Verify `PRAGMA compile_options`; preserve WAL and busy timeout. |
| JSON | `serde`, `serde_json` | Version all persisted envelopes. Use `serde_json::Value` only for explicitly opaque provider/plugin fields. |
| TOML | `toml` | Implement current merge semantics explicitly. |
| YAML | `serde_yml` or another maintained serde YAML parser | Needed for skills and pnpm workspace discovery. |
| Schema generation | `schemars` | Replaces Zod-to-JSON-Schema for tool definitions. |
| Input validation | typed `serde` DTOs plus `garde`/`validator` or manual validation | Manual validation is often clearer for path and risk policies. |
| IDs | `ulid` | Preserve textual ULID compatibility if desired. |
| Logging | `tracing`, `tracing-subscriber`, `tracing-appender` | Reproduce session/app separation and rotation semantics. |
| Tree-sitter/search | existing crates | Already selected and implemented. |
| ONNX | retain `tract-onnx` initially | `ort` may be faster/more compatible but often complicates one-binary distribution. |
| Local embedding tokenization | existing `tokenizers` | Already in use. |
| OAuth | `oauth2` | Device flow and PKCE; provider-specific adapters still required. |
| AWS | `aws-config` and AWS SDK/Smithy crates, or `aws-sigv4` plus Smithy EventStream | Official chain improves profile, SSO and role support but substantially increases build size. |
| Google auth | `yup-oauth2` or `gcp_auth` | Broader ADC support than the current service-account-only implementation. |
| Secure credentials | `keyring`, `secrecy`, `zeroize` | Keep a `0600` atomic-file fallback for headless Linux systems without a keyring service. |
| Process management | `tokio::process`, a vetted process-group wrapper, `nix` on Unix, Windows Job Objects | Must preserve process-tree cancellation, not merely kill the shell parent. |
| PTY support | `portable-pty` if interactive shell work is added | Not needed for parity with the current non-interactive shell tool. |
| LSP | `lsp-types` plus a small custom client | `tower-lsp` is primarily for implementing servers, not clients. |
| Testing | `cargo test`, `rstest`, `proptest`, `insta`, `wiremock`, `assert_cmd`, `predicates`, `tempfile` | Add PTY tests through `portable-pty`/`expectrl` and terminal snapshots through `vt100`. |
| Packaging | `cargo-dist`, `cargo-zigbuild`/`cross`, `cargo-binstall` | Can replace much of the Bun+napi release matrix. |

# 5. Benefits and risks specific to PRAANA

## Benefits

### Stronger message and provider-state modeling

Rust enums plus Serde are a good fit for:

- canonical message parts,
- tool-call/result correlation,
- provider-native opaque reasoning state,
- compaction control records,
- artifact references,
- versioned event envelopes.

This directly attacks the current use of `any`, `Record<string, unknown>`, ad hoc conversions and flattened prior history in `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/turn.ts`.

### Simpler standalone distribution

A full Rust executable can directly include:

- search,
- tree-sitter grammars,
- SQLite,
- embedding runtime.

That removes:

- Bun installation for source/global use,
- the package-scoped JSX transform,
- npm platform leaf packages,
- `praana-natives.node`,
- the native API mirror and loader.

### Better control of concurrency and cancellation

PRAANA currently has several independent process spawners with duplicated timeout and SIGTERM/SIGKILL behavior:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/tools/system.ts:180`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/tools/test-runner/spawn.ts:21`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/verify/spawn.ts:23`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/lsp/client.ts:110`

A shared Rust process supervisor could enforce one policy and use structured cancellation throughout the turn.

### Existing CPU-heavy pieces are already Rust

The risky algorithm selection for tree-sitter, search and ONNX has already happened. A full Rust core can absorb it rather than starting from zero.

## Risks

### The likely-to-change code is the largest code

The proposed history redesign touches:

- the 1.75K-line turn loop,
- both compilers,
- the event log,
- context-engine compiler and turn ledger,
- artifact ingestion,
- provider message serializers,
- resume,
- the UI transcript.

Porting those before redesign stabilization is likely throwaway work.

### UI parity is expensive

The TUI is close to 9K logical lines and depends on capabilities OpenTUI already supplies. Ratatui is mature, but PRAANA would own substantially more editor, layout and streaming-render behavior.

### Provider correctness is more important than memory safety

The custom drivers contain subtle protocol semantics that the Rust compiler cannot verify:

- SSE chunk boundaries,
- interleaved tool calls,
- usage accounting,
- retry-before-emission rules,
- Anthropic thinking signatures,
- Responses continuation state,
- Google thought signatures,
- Bedrock binary EventStream framing.

AI can generate Rust rapidly, but plausible-looking serializers are exactly where silent semantic failures occur.

### Existing tests are not directly portable

The 40.9K-line suite is nearly as large as the implementation. Heavy module mocking means a Rust port must first introduce traits and dependency injection. Deleting the TS tests while rewriting would discard the strongest available oracle.

### Rust plugin ABI and “one binary” pull in opposite directions

Native Rust dynamic libraries do not have a stable Rust ABI. Using `libloading` requires a C ABI, explicit ownership rules and per-platform binaries. WASM or subprocess plugins are safer but add runtime size or sidecar files.

### Performance gains may not be visible

Network latency and model generation dominate normal turns. Search and ONNX are already native. A Rust port should be justified by architecture, distribution and correctness—not expected dramatic turn-speed improvements.

---

# 6. Strategy comparison

| Strategy | Advantages | Main drawbacks | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Big-bang full rewrite** | Clean end state; one toolchain and executable; can discard obsolete architecture | Highest semantic risk; loses TS oracle; rewrites UI and two redesigns simultaneously; poor A/B attribution | **Not recommended now** |
| **Rust core + TS/OpenTUI UI** | Preserves the most expensive UX; Rust owns persistence/providers/tools; good migration bridge | Still requires Bun/OpenTUI; two-language packaging; N-API is awkward for streams | **Recommended transition** |
| **Keep TS, expand native Rust** | Lowest risk; existing boundary works; ideal for measured CPU-heavy primitives | Retains Bun transform, JS orchestration, sidecar release matrix; limited benefit for message-model redesign | Best choice if full Rust is not a firm goal |
| **Redesign in TS, then port** | Establishes semantics while tests still run; creates a reliable oracle; may reduce duplicated subsystems before port | Temporary double work and mixed-language period | **Recommended immediate strategy** |

For the transitional Rust-core approach, a long-lived **JSONL RPC subprocess** is preferable to expanding N-API for the stateful turn engine. N-API remains appropriate for pure synchronous primitives, but streaming callbacks, cancellation, panics and lifetime management become difficult when the whole core crosses that boundary.

# 7. Natural seams and incremental migration order

## Existing seams

Useful boundaries already exist:

- LLM strategy:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/llm/drivers/base.ts`
- UI event sink:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/ui-events.ts`
- Hook dispatcher:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/hooks/registry.ts`
- Context-engine facade:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/context-engine/index.ts`
- Embedder and summarizer interfaces:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/memory/types.ts:99`
- Native API:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/native/types.ts`
- Controller/UI boundary:  
  `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/app-controller.ts`

Weak seams include the concrete `MemoryStore`, the broad `Session` object, the `any`-based tool registry, and direct database access from unrelated subsystems.

## Recommended order

### Phase 0: establish the new semantics in TypeScript

1. Define a versioned canonical message log:
   - real user/assistant/tool messages,
   - typed content parts,
   - provider continuation metadata,
   - stable message and tool-call IDs,
   - compaction and reset records as append-only control events.
2. Make compaction a **projection** over the immutable log.
3. Store large content as host-owned artifacts; messages contain references.
4. Eliminate or formally derive the SQLite turn ledger and persisted UI transcript from the canonical log.
5. Define a language-neutral memory-plugin protocol.

Do not make classic compaction depend on Cognitive Memory. It currently does:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/auto-compact.ts:93`
- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/auto-compact.ts:110`

Session compaction should produce a host-owned session summary/artifact even when no cross-session memory plugin is installed.

### Phase 1: split and reuse the current Rust crate

Extract pure Rust search/tree-sitter/embed code from the N-API wrapper. Keep the wrapper temporarily so TypeScript continues using the same implementation.

### Phase 2: port deterministic pure logic

Port and compare:

- token estimation,
- BM25,
- cosine similarity,
- state graph,
- content classification,
- distillers,
- checkpoint reconciliation,
- context scoring,
- prompt assembly,
- redaction and risk classifiers.

These are suitable for byte-for-byte or structured differential testing.

### Phase 3: port persistence

Implement:

- canonical JSONL event store,
- artifact/context runtime SQLite,
- scorecard and workflow tables,
- schema migrations,
- crash/truncated-record recovery,
- WAL and busy-timeout behavior.

Read both TS-created and Rust-created fixtures during the transition.

### Phase 4: implement the memory plugin host

Move Cognitive Memory behind the language-neutral contract. Keep skill statistics and session/context telemetry host-owned.

### Phase 5: port provider drivers

Port one protocol at a time:

1. OpenAI-compatible
2. Anthropic
3. OpenAI Responses/Codex
4. Google/Vertex
5. Bedrock
6. Azure/custom-provider variations

Each should pass request-body and stream-event fixture parity before becoming active.

### Phase 6: port tools and hook orchestration

Preserve exact ordering:

- plan,
- validation,
- risk,
- circuit,
- write-path acquire,
- tool,
- LSP,
- verify,
- enrichment,
- redaction,
- circuit accounting,
- write-path release.

Reference:

- `/home/amit/projects/praana/src/hooks/index.ts:69`

Port shell/process behavior late because it is security- and platform-sensitive.

### Phase 7: Rust headless runner

Make the Rust core pass the deterministic headless suite before connecting the TUI. This is also the right A/B and Harbor surface.

### Phase 8: UI decision

Either:

- retain OpenTUI as a client of the Rust core, or
- rewrite in Ratatui after the core is stable.

The Ratatui rewrite should be treated as a separate UX project.
